front: What specific system does Birrell & Nelson's "Implementing Remote Procedure Calls" describe?
back: A specific RPC package built at Xerox PARC, covering the design options the authors faced and the decisions they made: structure, binding, the transport-level protocol, performance measurements, and optimizations to minimize load on servers with many clients.

front: In the Birrell & Nelson model, what happens to the caller and to other processes during a remote procedure call?
back: The caller is suspended, parameters are passed to the callee's environment, the procedure runs there, and results come back as from an ordinary return. While the caller is suspended, other processes on its machine may still run, depending on the parallelism of the environment.

front: What three attractions of the RPC idea do Birrell & Nelson list?
back:
• Clean and simple semantics
  • Efficiency (procedure calls seem simple enough for communication to be rapid)
  • Generality (procedures are the main intra-machine communication mechanism)

front: According to Birrell & Nelson, since when had the RPC idea been discussed, and whose work examined the design space?
back: The idea had been discussed in the literature since at least 1976; Nelson's doctoral dissertation is an extensive examination of the design space.

front: What two notable earlier full-scale RPC implementation efforts do Birrell & Nelson name?
back: Courier (Xerox NS protocol family) and work at MIT. Full-scale implementations were rarer than paper designs.

front: For what project was the Birrell & Nelson RPC work done?
back: The Cedar project. The authors believed they understood the designer's choices from earlier work (especially Nelson's thesis) but found several areas inadequately understood and produced a design with several novel aspects.

front: What major issues facing an RPC designer do Birrell & Nelson list?
back:
• Precise semantics under machine and communication failures
  • Semantics of address-containing arguments without a shared address space
  • Integration into existing/future programming systems
  • Binding (how a caller finds the callee's location and identity)
  • Transfer protocols for data and control
  • Data integrity and security on an open network

front: What two topics does the Birrell & Nelson paper explicitly defer to planned later papers?
back: Encryption-based security, and the detailed manufacture of stub modules.

front: What is Cedar, the environment for Birrell & Nelson's RPC work?
back: A large project to build a powerful, convenient programming environment with uniform, highly interactive user interfaces, for single-user workstations and also for building servers.

front: What was the Dorado, the main hardware for Birrell & Nelson's RPC work, and how fast was a local call on it?
back: A very powerful machine where a simple Algol-style call and return takes under 10 microseconds, with a 24-bit virtual address space (of 16-bit words) and an 80-megabyte disk. The authors liken a Dorado to an IBM 370/168 dedicated to one user.

front: Over what network did communication typically run in Birrell & Nelson's environment, and what were the typical offered loads?
back: Typically a 3-megabit-per-second Ethernet (some on 10 Mbit). The research internetwork had about 160 Ethernets connected by leased telephone and satellite links at 4800-56000 bps. Most traffic was on the local Ethernet; offered loads above 40 percent of Ethernet capacity were very rare, 10 percent typical.

front: What did the PUP family of protocols provide in Birrell & Nelson's environment?
back: Uniform internetwork access, including an unreliable datagram service and reliable flow-controlled byte streams; raw Ethernet packets are available between two machines on the same Ethernet.

front: What was the dominant programming language in Birrell & Nelson's Cedar environment?
back: Mesa (as modified for Cedar), with Smalltalk and InterLisp also used, and no assembly language for Dorados. Essentially all programming was in high-level languages.

front: What minimum average round-trip time did Birrell & Nelson give for a packet exchange on the 10 Mbit Ethernet?
back: 120 microseconds.

front: What was the primary purpose of Birrell & Nelson's RPC work?
back: To make distributed computation easy. The authors observed that building communicating programs was previously a task only for a select group of communication experts, and that existing communication mechanisms were a major factor constraining distributed computing.

front: According to Birrell & Nelson, what fundamental difficulties of distributed systems would remain even if RPC made communication as easy as local calls?
back: Timing, independent failure of components, and coexistence of independent execution environments.

text: Birrell & Nelson's efficiency aim was to keep RPC within about a factor of {{c1::five}} of the network's necessary transmission times, lest application designers avoid communication and distort their designs.

front: What design tension did Birrell & Nelson identify in their secondary aim of powerful semantics?
back: The tension between powerful semantics and efficiency (achieving powerful semantics without losing simplicity or efficiency).

front: Why was security a major aim for Birrell & Nelson, and what was the state of practice?
back: No previously implemented protocol protected data in transit (even passwords were sent as clear-text); secure end-to-end RPC had apparently never been built.

front: Why did Birrell & Nelson choose procedure calls over message passing?
back: The choice was not forced by their aims; they judged the two would not differ much in the problems faced, and chose procedure calls because that was the main control-and-data-transfer mechanism in Mesa.

front: What more-parallel paradigm did Birrell & Nelson consider and reject, and why?
back: A remote-fork paradigm; rejected because it would not change the major design problems.

front: Why did Birrell & Nelson discard emulating a shared address space among machines?
back: Possible difficulties were integrating remote addresses into the languages (and perhaps machine architecture) and achieving acceptable efficiency; a naive implementation would widen language addresses by the 16-bit PUP host address. They judged the cost would exceed the benefit on their hardware and assumed the absence of shared addresses.

front: What guiding principle governed Birrell & Nelson's remote-call semantics?
back: Remote-call semantics should be as close as possible to local-call semantics, to keep the facility easy to use for programmers familiar with single-machine use.

front: As a consequence of their local-semantics principle, how did Birrell & Nelson handle time-outs on a call's duration?
back: They used no time-out to limit a call's duration in the absence of failure, because local calls have no time-out and the languages already include mechanisms to abort an activity. This deviated from common practice.

front: Which binding semantics did Birrell & Nelson choose, versus those in Nelson's thesis?
back: Semantics based closely on the existing Cedar mechanisms (the binding scheme of Section 2), in preference to those in Nelson's thesis. The paper text literally says "building semantics described below"; the forward reference is to the binding section.

front: What is the RPCRuntime responsible for in Birrell & Nelson's design?
back: Retransmissions, acknowledgments, packet routing, and encryption.

front: What program generates the stubs in Birrell & Nelson's RPC, and from what?
back: A program called Lupine generates the stubs automatically from Mesa interface modules. These interface modules are the basis of Mesa/Cedar separate compilation and binding, and consist mainly of a list of procedure names with argument and result types.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's terminology, what do "exports" and "imports" mean for an interface?
back: A module implementing an interface's procedures exports it; a module calling them imports it. Lupine generates the user-stub (exporting the interface) and the server-stub (importing it).

front: What does Lupine generate, and what responsibilities remain with the programmer in Birrell & Nelson's design?
back: Lupine generates the packing/unpacking code and the dispatch to the correct procedure for an incoming call. The programmer must avoid arguments or results incompatible with the lack of a shared address space (Lupine checks this), and must invoke the binding and handle reported failures.

front: What are the two aspects of binding in Birrell & Nelson's scheme?
back:
• Naming: how a client specifies what it wants to bind to
  • Location: how a caller finds the callee's machine address and specifies the procedure
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: What are the two parts of an interface name in Birrell & Nelson's binding scheme?
back:
• The type: which interface the caller expects, at some level of abstraction (e.g. the abstraction "mail server")
  • The instance: which particular implementor (e.g. one particular mail server)
A reasonable default type name is derived from the Mesa interface module name.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: Who gives an interface name its meaning in Birrell & Nelson's binding scheme, and does the RPC package enforce it?
back: The semantics of an interface name are an agreement between the exporter and the importer; the RPC package does not fully enforce them.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: What distributed database does Birrell & Nelson's RPC use for binding, and why?
back: Grapevine. Its attraction is being widely and reliably available, distributed across multiple servers and keeping at least three copies of each entry, so lookups almost never fail. The alternatives (hard-coding network addresses, or broadcast) were judged unsatisfactory.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: What two kinds of Grapevine entry exist, and how does the RPC package map interface names onto them?
back: Entries are keyed by a character-string RName. Individuals have a connect-site (a network address); groups have a member-list of RNames. The RPC package keeps two entries per interface name: the instance is an individual whose connect-site is the exporting machine's address; the type is a group whose members are the instances of that type.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: In Birrell & Nelson's worked naming example, what are the type and the instances, and how do they appear in Grapevine?
back: Type FileAccess.Alpine is a Grapevine group listing two instances: Ebbets.Alpine (exported from address 3#22#) and Luther.Alpine (from 3#276#). Each instance is an individual whose connect-site is its address, e.g. Ebbets.Alpine has connect-site 3#22#.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: What does the server-stub call to export an interface in Birrell & Nelson's design, and what is the optimization?
back: It calls ExportInterface in RPCRuntime with the interface name and a dispatcher procedure; ExportInterface updates Grapevine so the instance is in the type group and has the right connect-site. As an optimization, the database is not updated if already correct, which is usually the case.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: What does the exporting machine's RPCRuntime record per exported interface in Birrell & Nelson's design?
back: A table holding the interface name, the dispatcher, and a 32-bit permanently-unique machine-relative identifier of the export; the table is an array indexed by a small integer.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: How is the 32-bit export identifier kept unique in Birrell & Nelson's design, and what rate does that constrain?
back: By successive values of a 32-bit counter initialized on start-up to a one-second real-time clock, which constrains the average rate of ExportInterface calls to under one per second since restart (burst rate can exceed this).
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: What does the user-stub call to import an interface, and what does the import procedure do in Birrell & Nelson's design?
back: It calls ImportInterface with the desired type and instance; RPCRuntime asks Grapevine for the connect-site, then makes a remote call to that machine's RPCRuntime for the binding information. If the machine is not exporting the interface, binding fails; otherwise its table yields the unique identifier and table index, returned and remembered by the user-stub.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: On a subsequent call in Birrell & Nelson's design, what does the call packet carry and how does the callee use it?
back: The call packet carries the unique identifier, the table index, and the entry-point number of the procedure. The callee's RPCRuntime looks up the table by index, verifies the unique identifier matches, and passes the packet to the dispatcher.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: What happens if an importer specifies only the type (no instance) in Birrell & Nelson's binding?
back: RPCRuntime enumerates the group members and tries their addresses "in an order which tends to locate the closest (most responsive) running exporter", binding to the closest instance of a replicated service.
source: Section 2.1-2.2: Binding, naming, and locating an exporter

front: Why is it advantageous in Birrell & Nelson's scheme that importing an interface has no effect on the exporting machine's data structures?
back: It is advantageous for servers with hundreds of users and avoids questions about what the server should do on importer crashes.
source: Section 2.3: Discussion of the binding scheme

front: How and why are bindings implicitly broken in Birrell & Nelson's scheme when an exporter crashes and restarts?
back: Because the unique identifier's currency is checked on every call. The authors argue this implicit unbinding is correct, since otherwise a user would not be notified of a between-calls crash.
source: Section 2.3: Discussion of the binding scheme

front: Why did Birrell & Nelson reject the more efficient alternative of handing importers the exporter's internal dispatcher representation?
back: It would allow unchecked access to almost any procedure and defeat protection/security. Their scheme allows calls only on explicitly exported procedures.
source: Section 2.3: Discussion of the binding scheme

front: What role do Grapevine's access controls play in Birrell & Nelson's binding security?
back: They restrict who can export particular interface names, which the authors call the desired semantics (a random user should not be able to claim to be a mail server and intercept traffic); for replicated services this access control is critical to secure two-way authentication.
source: Section 2.3: Discussion of the binding scheme

front: List Birrell & Nelson's binding-time choices from most to least flexible.
back:
1. Type only (instance decided dynamically)
  2. Instance as an RName (most common, delaying the choice of machine)
  3. Instance as a network address (binding to a machine at compile time)
There are also facilities to dynamically instantiate and import interfaces, useful in open-ended algorithms such as a distributed-transaction manager.
source: Section 2.3: Discussion of the binding scheme

front: At what grain does Birrell & Nelson's scheme allow binding, and why not finer?
back: Binding is not allowed at a finer grain than an entire interface; finer-grained binding was not considered useful in the systems observed.
source: Section 2.3: Discussion of the binding scheme

front: Why did Birrell & Nelson design a specialized packet protocol for RPC instead of reusing an existing byte-stream protocol?
back: RPC semantics could be achieved over PUP byte streams (as the NS "Courier" RPC protocol uses the NS sequenced packet protocol), but their measurements and experience convinced them this was unsatisfactory: a transport protocol designed specially for RPC could gain a factor of ten in performance.

front: What two design emphases drove Birrell & Nelson's RPC transport protocol?
back:
• Minimize elapsed real-time between initiating a call and getting results (unlike bulk-transfer protocols where transfer time dominates)
  • Minimize the load a server bears from many clients, so expensive connection setup/teardown and large per-connection state are unacceptable

front: In Birrell & Nelson's protocol, under what conditions is a call aborted, and under what conditions is it not?
back: Provided the server RPCRuntime still responds, there is no upper bound on how long results are awaited. A call is aborted on communication breakdown or crash, but not if the server code deadlocks or loops, which is identical to local-call semantics.

front: What common case does Birrell & Nelson's "simple call" optimize for?
back: All arguments fit in one packet, all results fit in one packet, and calls are frequent. The caller sends a call packet (call identifier, data specifying the procedure, arguments); the callee invokes the procedure and sends a result packet with the same call identifier and the results.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's simple-call protocol, how many packets are sent per call in the common case, and how is acknowledgment handled?
back: The transmitter retransmits until acknowledged, but the result of a call acknowledges the call packet and the next call packet acknowledges the previous result packet. So when call duration and inter-call interval are each less than the retransmission interval, exactly two packets are sent per call (one each way). Longer calls or gaps add up to two more packets.

front: What does the call identifier do in Birrell & Nelson's protocol, and what are its parts?
back: It lets the caller confirm a result is for its current call (not a delayed earlier result) and lets the callee eliminate duplicate call packets. It consists of the permanent globally-unique calling machine identifier, a machine-relative calling-process identifier, and a sequence number. The pair [machine, process] is an activity.

front: What key property of each activity does Birrell & Nelson's protocol rely on, and how is duplicate elimination done?
back: Each activity has at most one outstanding remote call at a time (it will not start a new call until it receives the previous result). The sequence number must be monotonic per activity (not necessarily sequential). The callee RPCRuntime keeps a table of the last sequence number per calling activity; a call packet whose sequence number is not greater than the table value is discarded as a duplicate.

front: What is a "connection" in Birrell & Nelson's protocol, and how is it established?
back: The shared state between a calling activity and the server machine's RPCRuntime. No establishment handshake is needed: receipt of a call packet from a new activity creates the connection implicitly.

front: What does an idle connection cost in Birrell & Nelson's protocol?
back: Only a sequence-number table entry at the server and a single machine-wide counter at the caller; no pinging is used to maintain idle connections.

front: How is a connection terminated in Birrell & Nelson's protocol?
back: There is no explicit termination: the server may discard idle connection state after, say, five minutes, without interacting with the caller.

front: What is the conversation identifier in Birrell & Nelson's protocol, and how is it generated?
back: A 32-bit identifier (used for secure calls) that distinguishes incarnations of a calling machine, so a restarted machine's sequence numbers are not mistakenly treated as duplicates. It is generated from a 32-bit clock initialized from network time servers at restart.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's protocol, what lets duplicate elimination cope with a server that crashes and restarts while a caller retransmits?
back: The per-export unique identifier, checked on every call.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's protocol, how is a probe packet used while awaiting a result?
back: While awaiting a result the caller periodically sends a probe packet the callee must acknowledge, so the caller notices a crashed callee or serious communication failure; as long as probes are acknowledged the caller waits indefinitely.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's complicated calls, how is a retransmitted packet modified, and what situations does this handle?
back: It is modified to request an explicit acknowledgment; this handles lost packets, long-duration calls, and long gaps between calls.

front: Describe the probe timing schedule in Birrell & Nelson's complicated-call protocol.
back: The first probe is sent after slightly more than the approximate round-trip time; the interval grows gradually until, after about 10 minutes, probes are sent every five minutes; each probe is retransmitted like other packets. This detects only communication-level failures, not a callee deadlocked on the call.

front: What alternative to probing did Birrell & Nelson consider and reject?
back: The recipient spontaneously generating an acknowledgment when it will not produce the next packet in time; rejected because the saved packet was judged not worth the extra server-side data structure and process cost.

front: How does Birrell & Nelson's protocol handle arguments or results that exceed one packet?
back: They are sent in multiple packets, each but the last requesting an explicit acknowledgment; caller and callee alternate (data packet, acknowledgment), which lets the implementation use only one packet buffer per end and avoids bulk-transfer buffering/flow control. Each data packet within a call has a call-relative sequence number for duplicate elimination.

front: What inefficiency do Birrell & Nelson acknowledge in their multi-packet calls, and how do they respond to it?
back: The protocol sends more packets than logically required (up to twice as many as a good bulk-data protocol, since each packet is acknowledged), which is poor across long-haul networks with large delays. They keep RPC and bulk data as separate protocols, note RPC can carry bulk data by multiplexing single-packet calls across processes, and leave unexplored the option of switching to a conventional protocol for complicated calls.

front: What are Mesa signals, and how do they behave when raised?
back: Mesa's elaborate exception facilities, thought of as dynamically bound procedure activations. Raising a signal makes the runtime scan the call stack for a catch phrase, which may return (resuming where the exception was raised) or jump out (unwinding newer activations most-recent-first).

front: How does Birrell & Nelson's RPC package emulate Mesa signals across machines?
back: The server can send an exception packet in place of a result packet; the caller's RPCRuntime handles it like a call packet but raises the exception in the appropriate process; a catch phrase that returns sends results back to the callee; one that jumps notifies the callee to unwind. The callee may communicate only exceptions declared in the exported Mesa interface.

front: Why does Birrell & Nelson's design restrict the callee to communicating only exceptions declared in the exported interface?
back: It simplifies name translation and aids protection and debugging.

front: What is the "call failed" exception in Birrell & Nelson's RPC, and what is its significance?
back: In addition to callee-raised exceptions, RPCRuntime may raise a call failed exception on communication difficulty; this is the primary way clients tell remote from local calls.

front: How expensive were process forking and swapping in Mesa/Cedar, per Birrell & Nelson?
back: Forking costs about as much as ten local procedure calls, and a process swap swaps an evaluation stack and one register plus invalidating cached information. On the scale of a remote call these costs matter, so the authors kept them low.

front: How does Birrell & Nelson's design avoid process-creation cost per call?
back: Each machine keeps a stock of idle server processes; a finished server process reverts to idle rather than dying, and excess idle processes created during a peak kill themselves.

front: How is an incoming packet dispatched to a process in Birrell & Nelson's design?
back: Each packet carries source and destination process identifiers; an interrupt handler dispatches an incoming packet directly to a waiting process if the destination process is waiting, otherwise to an idle server process; a new call reuses the identifier of the process that handled the activity's previous call (likely still waiting to acknowledge).

front: How many process swaps does a simple call typically involve in Birrell & Nelson's design, and why not fewer?
back: Simple calls create no processes and involve typically four process swaps. The theoretical minimum without busy-waiting is two; the extra two arise because an interrupt handler, not device microcode, dispatches incoming packets.

front: Summarize the optimizations Birrell & Nelson adopted in their RPC.
back:
• Implicit acknowledgment via subsequent packets
  • Minimizing connection-maintenance cost
  • Avoiding connection setup/teardown
  • Reducing process switches

front: What "cheating" optimization do Birrell & Nelson use when caller and callee are on the same network?
back: RPC packets bypass the normal protocol-hierarchy software layers (the network driver treats RPC packets as a special case); the internetwork protocol hierarchy is still used for internetwork routing. The authors call this cheating that works only because RPC is the special case, but argue a particular transport protocol can gain significantly by bypassing lower-layer generality.

front: What reasonable optimizations did Birrell & Nelson deliberately NOT use, and what might they have gained?
back: Avoiding the internet packet format on the local network, specialized packet formats for simple calls, special-purpose network microcode, forbidding non-RPC communication, and busy-waits instead of process swaps. Using them might have given another factor of two in performance.

front: What does Birrell & Nelson's encryption-based security provide, and what underlies it?
back: It uses Grapevine as the authentication service / key distribution center and the federal Data Encryption Standard; callers and callees are mutually assured of identity; full end-to-end encryption protects against eavesdropping and detects modification, replay, or creation of calls. The details are deferred to a later paper.

front: On what hardware and network were Birrell & Nelson's performance figures measured?
back: Between two Dorados running Cedar on a lightly loaded 2.94-megabit Ethernet.

front: How did Birrell & Nelson time their RPC measurements, and how accurate were they?
back: By counting Dorado microprocessor cycles and dividing by the crystal frequency, accurate to within about ten percent; times are elapsed times over 12,000 calls per procedure.

front: What interval does a Birrell & Nelson Table I time cover?
back: From the user's invocation of the user-stub procedure through its return: both stubs, both RPCRuntimes, the server implementation, and transmission both ways. No encryption was used.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's Table I, what were the minimum/median times for a call with no args/results, versus transmission and local-only times?
back: No args/results: 1059 microseconds min, 1097 median, 131 transmission, 9 local-only.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's Table I, what were the min/median times for a 10 args/results call?
back: 10 args/results: 1222 min / 1278 median / 239 transmission / 17 local-only.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's Table I, what were the min/median times for a 100-word array call?
back: 100-word array: 2915 min / 2926 median / 1219 transmission / 98 local-only.

front: In Birrell & Nelson's Table I, what were the min/median times for the resume-exception case?
back: 2555 min / 2637 median microseconds (284 transmission, 134 local-only).

front: In Birrell & Nelson's Table I, what were the min/median times for the unwind-exception case?
back: 3374 min / 3467 median microseconds (284 transmission, 196 local-only).

front: What did the twelve measured procedures in Birrell & Nelson's Table I consist of?
back: The first five had 0, 1, 2, 4, 10 arguments and the same number of results, each 16 bits; the next five had one array argument/result of 1, 4, 10, 40, 100 words; the last two raise an exception the caller resumes, and one the caller unwinds.

front: What peak throughput did Birrell & Nelson reach by interleaving parallel calls, and how did it compare to byte streams?
back: By interleaving parallel calls from multiple processes they reached 2 megabits/second transferring between Dorado main memories on the 3 Mbit Ethernet, equal to their best byte-stream implementation (written in BCPL).

front: What did Birrell & Nelson say about the cost of export/import, which they did not measure?
back: Export/import cost is dominated by talking to Grapevine, which they did not measure; after locating the exporter, getting the dispatcher identifier uses one RPC with a few words of data.

front: How large was the RPCRuntime implementation in Birrell & Nelson's paper?
back: The whole RPCRuntime is four Cedar modules (packet exchange, packet sequencing, binding, security) totalling about 2,200 lines; Lupine is substantially larger. The package was fully implemented and in use by Cedar programmers.

front: What clients used Birrell & Nelson's RPC, and for which other languages did protocol implementations exist?
back: Clients: Alpine (a file server supporting multimachine transactions), the control communication for an Ethernet telephone/audio project, and two network games with real-time communication. Protocol implementations existed for BCPL, InterLisp, SmallTalk, and C.

front: When did Birrell & Nelson say RPC seems the wrong paradigm, and what open question did they raise?
back: RPC seems wrong in cases where multicasting or broadcasting is more appropriate. They raised the open question of whether a general-purpose transport protocol could reach RPC-level performance (they had not seen it achieved).

front: What contributions of general interest did Birrell & Nelson claim for their work?
back: A particular point in the RPC design spectrum; good performance without extreme measures; transport-connection management that minimizes cost and server state; and powerful-yet-simple binding semantics that were easy and efficient to implement.
